strengths: The pipeline—motion tokenization, LLM-based action decomposition, supervised cold start, and GRPO refinement—is clearly presented.
Applying explicit planning and reinforcement learning to compositional text-to-motion generation is timely and potentially useful.
HumanML3D results are competitive, including the best reported R-Precision@2/@3, MM-Dist, and Diversity among the listed methods.
The component ablation covers all combinations of CoT, semantic reward, and motion reward, with the complete model performing best overall.
The qualitative analysis targets complex and out-of-distribution prompts, where structured action decomposition is plausibly beneficial.
weaknesses: The central claims about out-of-distribution generalization, long-horizon coherence, controllability, and reasoning are not convincingly evaluated. Evidence is limited to a few selected static visualizations against one baseline, without a defined OOD benchmark, quantitative evaluation, or human study.
Although the paper claims evaluation on HumanML3D and KIT-ML, it reports quantitative results and ablations only for HumanML3D.

The evaluation is insufficiently independent of the training rewards. Semantic reward uses the same embedding family underlying standard alignment metrics, while motion reward compares against paired ground-truth motion. This may directly optimize benchmark proxies without demonstrating perceptual quality or genuine reasoning.

There is no evidence that the generated Chain-of-Thought is faithful, necessary, or causally useful. The paper does not evaluate intermediate plans or compare against concise action plans, caption augmentation, equally sized supervised training without CoT, or GRPO without emitted reasoning.

The MotionCoT pipeline is under-specified and weakly validated. Dataset size, exact prompts, filtering thresholds, regeneration statistics, failure rates, and human quality checks are absent. DeepSeek-R1 both generates and judges traces, creating correlated-error risk.

Reproducibility is poor: tokenizer configuration, reward aggregation, GRPO group size, sampling parameters, KL coefficient, optimizer, learning rates, batch sizes, training duration, GPU count, and inference settings are missing. Code and data are only promised.

The method description is inconsistent: some sections use <think>, <output>, and <Motion>, while the format reward requires only <think> and <Motion>. The paper also claims operation without explicit reward functions immediately before defining three explicit rewards.

The quantitative claims are overstated. Motion-R1 is not best on R-Precision@1, FID, or MModality, and it is unclear whether baselines were rerun identically or copied from prior work. No paired significance analysis is provided.
The ablation lacks a clean base-model/no-component condition and does not separate gains from synthetic CoT data, additional supervised fine-tuning, GRPO itself, and reward design.

Static pose montages cannot substantiate claims about smoothness, temporal ordering, complete trajectories, or long-term coherence. Reference [9] is also inconsistently called MotionAgent and MotionLLM.

The contribution appears primarily to combine established ingredients—VQ-VAE motion tokens, LLM-generated plans, synthetic supervision, and GRPO with hand-designed rewards—in a new domain. Stronger controls and evaluation are needed to establish top-tier novelty and significance.
Biases and failure modes inherited from LLM-generated plans, physical plausibility, and potential misuse are not discussed.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive combination of structured action decomposition, motion tokenization, and GRPO-based optimization for text-to-motion generation.
The method is evaluated against numerous established baselines on HumanML3D and reports competitive retrieval, distributional, and diversity metrics.
The component ablation includes CoT, semantic reward, and motion reward variants, providing some evidence that the full training recipe is more effective than its individual components.
The presentation is generally readable, and the pipeline and reward definitions are easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central claims about complex-instruction reasoning, long-horizon coherence, controllability, and out-of-distribution generalization are not convincingly evaluated. Evidence consists mainly of two cherry-picked OOD visualizations against one baseline, with no quantitative benchmark, human evaluation, systematic prompt set, or statistical analysis. Static pose montages cannot establish temporal coherence or motion quality.
The paper claims evaluation on both HumanML3D and KIT-ML, but reports results only for HumanML3D. This directly undermines the repeated claim of extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks.

The standard HumanML3D metrics largely assess in-distribution generation and text-motion embedding alignment; they do not demonstrate that the generated CoT is faithful, causally useful, interpretable, or genuinely performs reasoning. No action-plan accuracy, reasoning-quality, compositionality, or plan-motion consistency metric is provided.

The reward encoders are also closely related to the encoders underlying standard text-to-motion evaluation. Optimizing cosine similarity in this feature space and then reporting retrieval/MM-Dist-style metrics from the same evaluation ecosystem creates a risk of evaluator overfitting and weakens the evidence of perceptual improvement.

Novelty is limited: the system mainly combines a conventional VQ-VAE motion tokenizer, synthetic LLM-generated decompositions, supervised fine-tuning, and an existing GRPO objective. The paper does not identify a substantial motion-specific algorithmic innovation beyond the chosen reward terms.

The ablation does not isolate the claimed benefit of reasoning adequately. CoT alone performs poorly, while the strong result appears only with the entire recipe; there is no matched direct-generation baseline with equal model, data, compute, and RL training, nor controls using concise action labels, captions, or randomly structured intermediate text.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Essential details are absent, including MotionCoT dataset size and filtering acceptance rates, complete prompts, tokenizer architecture and codebook settings, SFT/RL schedules, group size, sampling parameters, reward aggregation or ranking procedure, reward weights, clipping and KL coefficients, optimizer settings, and computational cost. The promised project link is blank, and code/data are only said to become available.

The description of GRPO is internally unclear: the paper says it avoids explicit reward functions and that rewards are used through groupwise preference ranking, yet it immediately defines explicit scalar rewards and a normalized scalar advantage. How the three rewards and format failures are combined into each sample's scalar reward is unspecified.

The motion-similarity reward depends on paired ground-truth motion, limiting the claimed general RL formulation and potentially encouraging imitation of a single reference despite claims of one-to-many diversity. This tension is not analyzed.

Qualitative comparisons are restricted to MotionLLM despite the quantitative table containing several stronger baselines, and there is no evidence that compared outputs use matched sampling budgets, seeds, or selection procedures. Overall, the reported standard-benchmark gains do not compensate for the missing evidence behind the paper's main reasoning and generalization contribution.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive framework that combines structured action decomposition, motion tokenization, supervised cold-start training, and GRPO-based refinement for text-to-motion generation.

Results on HumanML3D are promising: Motion-R1 obtains strong R-Precision, MM-Dist, and diversity, with confidence intervals from repeated evaluations and comparisons against several established baselines.
The component ablation covers CoT supervision and both proposed similarity rewards, and the full combination performs consistently well across the reported metrics.
The paper is generally clear, and its qualitative examples help communicate the intended benefits for compositional and abstract prompts.
weaknesses: The central claims about complex reasoning and out-of-distribution generalization are supported only by a few selected qualitative examples. There is no quantitative OOD benchmark, compositional evaluation, human study, or systematic assessment of whether all requested sub-actions are executed in the correct order.

The paper states that experiments cover HumanML3D and KIT-ML, but reports quantitative results only for HumanML3D. This makes the multiple-benchmark claim unsupported and substantially narrows the evidence.

The semantic and motion rewards use the same pretrained text-motion embedding framework underlying several evaluation metrics. Optimizing these representations and then evaluating with closely related representations creates a risk of metric overfitting; independent perceptual, physical-realism, or human-preference evaluation is needed.

The experiments do not convincingly establish that explicit CoT reasoning is the source of the gains. There is no matched conventional-planning baseline, inference-time intervention on the generated plans, assessment of plan correctness, or comparison against an otherwise identical model trained without textual rationales. The ablation therefore demonstrates component correlation more than causal reasoning benefits.

The GRPO formulation and implementation are underspecified: the paper does not clearly define how multiple rewards are combined, group size, reward weights, sampling settings, optimization hyperparameters, training duration, or token-level policy ratios. It also inconsistently claims GRPO avoids explicit reward functions while immediately introducing hand-designed rewards.

Reproducibility is currently weak. The project-page field is empty, code/model/data are only promised, and essential details of the CoT prompt, filtering criteria, regenerated-sample statistics, dataset size, tokenizer configuration, and compute budget are absent from the provided manuscript.

The technical novelty is limited: the tokenizer and language-model formulation follow prior work, while CoT distillation and GRPO are largely transferred from LLM training. Given the missing OOD validation and incomplete experimental reporting, the evidence is insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier venue despite the promising idea and HumanML3D results.

strengths: The paper targets an important text-to-motion problem and presents an intuitive two-stage framework combining LLM-generated action decompositions with reinforcement learning.
The method is evaluated on HumanML3D, KIT-ML, and BABEL, with reported improvements in several retrieval, alignment, and distributional metrics.
The component ablation covers combinations of decomposed CoT supervision, semantic reward, and motion reward, showing that the full configuration performs best.
The manuscript is generally understandable, includes training-compute information and prompts, and provides qualitative examples for compositional instructions.
weaknesses: The evaluation is substantially circular: the semantic and motion rewards use the pretrained Guo et al. embedding encoders that also underlie key reported metrics such as R-Precision and MM-Dist. Optimizing these encoders and then evaluating primarily through them does not establish better perceptual quality or semantic correctness. Independent encoders, physical-quality measures, and human evaluation are needed.

The central baselines are incomplete. MotionRL and MotionCritic motivate the work but are absent from the quantitative comparison. Baseline coverage also changes across datasets; for example, strong methods such as MoMask and MotionGPT-2 are omitted on KIT-ML. Consequently, the state-of-the-art claims are not convincingly supported.

The claimed OOD generalization rests on only a few hand-selected visualizations, without a defined OOD benchmark, quantitative evaluation, human study, or uncertainty analysis. Interpretability and the accuracy of the generated reasoning traces are likewise not evaluated.

The ablation lacks a clear standard direct-generation SFT baseline with neither CoT nor RL, and does not separate the effects of extra synthetic supervision, longer output sequences, GRPO itself, and the proposed reward construction. The CoT-only configuration is also markedly weaker than published baselines.

Important methodological details are missing: the scalar reward composition and weights are unspecified, as are the amount and filtering rate of synthetic CoT data, quality-control thresholds, LLM sampling settings, tokenizer architecture and codebook parameters, training duration in steps or epochs, decoding settings, and random seeds. A promise of future code release does not resolve current reproducibility concerns.

The novelty is limited: caption decomposition through an external LLM, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO with cosine-similarity rewards are individually standard, while the paper provides limited technical analysis showing that their combination constitutes a substantive advance.

Several claims overreach the evidence. No efficiency comparison supports the assertion that RL Binding is simpler or more scalable than prior RL methods; diversity exceeding ground truth on BABEL is interpreted as realistic without supporting evidence; and temporal or causal reasoning is asserted without targeted evaluation.

The metric description contains a consequential inconsistency: MM-Dist is described as cosine similarity while the tables treat lower values as better, whereas the standard metric is embedding distance. This further obscures the relationship between training rewards and evaluation.

Using similarity to a single paired ground-truth motion as a reward may encourage imitation or memorization and conflict with the intrinsically multimodal nature of text-to-motion generation, but this tradeoff is not analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem and presents an intuitive two-stage framework combining structured language-based planning with motion-token generation and reinforcement learning.

Experiments cover HumanML3D, KIT-ML, and BABEL. Several reported results are competitive, including improved MM-Dist on HumanML3D and strong retrieval/FID results on KIT-ML and BABEL. The authors report confidence intervals over 20 evaluation runs.

The manuscript is generally well organized, with useful pipeline diagrams, component ablations, prompts, compute information, and an ethics discussion. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/fed68c05af154209a6a0d4428a0140c0/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The evaluation is substantially circular. The semantic and motion rewards use the pretrained Guo et al. text-motion encoders that also underlie the principal R-Precision, MM-Dist, FID, and diversity evaluations. Directly optimizing representations used by the evaluator can improve these metrics without establishing better perceptual motion quality. Independent encoders, physical metrics, and blinded human evaluation are needed.

The claimed out-of-distribution generalization is supported only by a few selected qualitative examples against one baseline. Static snapshots cannot substantiate temporal coherence, smoothness, causality, or successful execution of multi-stage instructions. There is no systematic OOD benchmark, human preference study, or failure analysis.

The central claim that decomposed chain-of-thought causes improved reasoning or interpretability is not established. The paper provides no evaluation of plan correctness, faithfulness, or correspondence between individual plan steps and generated motion. The ablation also changes the supervision and output format, so it does not isolate reasoning from additional LLM-generated training text or extra computation.

Novelty is limited. The approach largely combines an established VQ-VAE motion tokenizer, LLM-generated action decomposition, supervised fine-tuning, GRPO, and cosine-similarity rewards. “RL Binding” appears to be a straightforward use of fixed evaluator similarities as rewards, with little technical analysis distinguishing it from standard reward shaping.

Important comparisons are missing despite motivating the work through RL-based methods: MotionRL and MotionCritic are not included experimentally. HumanML3D results are mixed rather than uniformly state of the art—Top-1 R-Precision trails MoMask, and FID is much worse than MoMask and T2M-GPT—while the prose repeatedly makes broad superiority claims.

The ablation study is difficult to interpret. It lacks a clearly identified matched SFT-only baseline without generated CoT, does not explain how no-CoT RL variants remain stable despite the earlier assertion that pure RL fails, and incorrectly describes strongly differing ablations as having “comparable performance.” No statistical significance analysis is given for component gains.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper omits the size and composition of the MotionCoT data, filtering thresholds and acceptance rates, the exact DeepSeek-R1 configuration, reward aggregation weights, training duration in steps or epochs, sampling settings, and key tokenizer architecture parameters. Code is only promised for the future.

There are technical and presentation inconsistencies: the appendix describes MM-Dist as cosine similarity although the standard metric is an embedding distance and lower is marked better; the stated output format alternates among <think>/<output>/<Motion>, <think>/<Motion>, and traces containing only <think>; and the GRPO objective is underspecified at the token level. These issues reduce confidence that the method and evaluation are precisely documented.

The BABEL evidence requires stronger validation. Its protocol is insufficiently explained, the comparison set differs substantially from the other benchmarks, and diversity exceeding ground-truth diversity is treated as inherently beneficial even though it may also reflect unrealistic or off-distribution motion. Overall, the promising numerical results do not overcome the evaluation leakage and lack of evidence for the paper’s main reasoning and generalization claims.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and practically appealing two-stage framework combining synthetic action decomposition with GRPO-based optimization; avoiding a separately trained human-preference model could reduce annotation cost.

Results span HumanML3D, KIT-ML, and BABEL. Motion-R1 obtains strong retrieval/alignment results, particularly R-Precision@2/3 and MM-Dist on HumanML3D, R-Precision and FID on KIT-ML, and all reported metrics on BABEL.
The component ablation covers the decomposed-CoT data and both alignment rewards, and the reported confidence intervals and compute costs are useful additions.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and its diagrams clearly communicate the overall training pipeline.
weaknesses: The evaluation is substantially circular: the semantic and motion rewards use the pretrained encoders from Guo et al. (2022a), while R-Precision, MM-Dist, FID, and Diversity are evaluated in closely related embedding spaces. Optimizing these representations can directly improve the reported metrics without establishing perceptual realism or semantic correctness. Independent encoders, physical-quality metrics, and human evaluation are needed.

The central claims about compositional reasoning, interpretability, and out-of-distribution generalization are supported only by a few selected static visualizations. There is no quantitative OOD benchmark, human preference study, or test showing that the emitted reasoning is faithful or causally used by the motion decoder.

The most relevant RL baselines, MotionRL and MotionCritic, are discussed but omitted from the quantitative comparisons. This prevents substantiating the claimed advantages in simplicity, efficiency, and performance over existing RL-based motion-generation methods.

Important implementation details are missing: the paper never specifies how the three rewards are combined or weighted; it omits the amount and composition of generated CoT data, quality-control thresholds, regeneration procedure, tokenizer configuration, training steps, decoding settings, and several preprocessing details. Code is only promised, limiting current reproducibility.

The ablation results contain unexplained behavior: combining the two rewards without CoT is no better in R-Precision and markedly worse in FID than using either reward alone. The paper nevertheless describes the variants as comparable and does not analyze this apparent optimization interaction.

Several conclusions overstate the evidence. On HumanML3D, Motion-R1 is not best in Top-1 R-Precision or FID, and its qualitative figures cannot demonstrate smoothness or temporal coherence. The BABEL diversity exceeding ground truth is also interpreted as unequivocally beneficial, although it may reflect distribution mismatch or artifacts.

Because the strongest numerical evidence may arise from reward/evaluation coupling and the claimed reasoning and OOD benefits lack controlled validation, the current submission is not yet competitive at the stated top-tier acceptance bar despite its promising direction.
